title: Underdog’s New 32MB AI Voice Model Works Without Internet
summary: Underdog launches 32MB offline voice model working without internet
detailed: AI startup Underdog launched Woof, a text-to-speech model with approximately 31 million parameters occupying 31.7MB of storage.
The model runs entirely locally on everyday phones or computers without requiring an internet connection or cloud servers.
Underdog created an interactive retro browser game called Escape to demonstrate the model by converting user-typed text into spoken audio.
This matters because it offers a private, lightweight alternative to cloud-based voice generation for consumer hardware and offline assistants.
sentences: AI startup Underdog has released Woof, a new text-to-speech model that is just 32MB in size and can generate speech directly on a phone or computer without relying on cloud servers.
The company has also launched a free browser-based game to demonstrate the model’s capabilities, allowing users to type text and hear it spoken aloud.

Unlike large AI models that require powerful servers, Woof is designed to run locally on everyday devices, potentially offering a more private and lightweight alternative to cloud-based voice generation.
Woof contains approximately 31 million parameters and occupies just 31.7MB of storage.
According to Underdog, the model can run on most devices without an internet connection once the necessary files are available locally.
This means speech generation can take place directly on a user’s device rather than requiring text to be sent to a remote server.
The company has made the model available for anyone to download.
Its relatively small size could make it suitable for applications such as offline voice assistants, text-to-speech tools, and personalized audio content.
However, the model’s small size does not necessarily mean it can match the capabilities or quality of much larger AI systems.

Underdog has created an interactive browser game called Escape to demonstrate Woof’s speech generation capabilities.
The game takes place in a retro-themed room featuring a typewriter, an old CRT monitor, a desk lamp, and a music tuner.
Players can type messages using the virtual typewriter, and Woof will convert the text into spoken audio.
The game also allows users to interact with other objects, including a music tuner that produces different sounds and music.
Its introduction refers to intrusive cloud providers, reflecting Underdog’s focus on running AI models locally instead of depending on external servers.
Woof follows the company’s earlier release of Bark, a 167MB speech-to-text model designed for transcription and dictation on local devices.
While Woof converts written text into speech, Bark performs the opposite function by converting spoken words into text.
Underdog has also introduced a 27-billion-parameter AI model designed to run on laptops.
The startup is developing a separate application that will allow users to interact with locally hosted AI models as an alternative to cloud-based assistants.

Underdog founder Sigil Wen told TechCrunch that he started developing these tools because he wanted an AI system that could run on his own devices and give users greater control over their information.
The company’s goal is to reduce dependence on cloud computing while making capable AI tools available on existing consumer hardware.

Although larger AI models still offer advantages for complex tasks, Underdog’s latest release demonstrates how smaller models can handle specific functions, such as speech generation, without requiring powerful remote infrastructure.
